en: Adhikāra 1:
Having bowed to the noble Mañjuśrī, the moon of gnosis who abides throughout the three times,
as well as to his *Nāmasaṃgīti*, which possesses profound and vast qualities;
Having examined the Yoga, Caryā, and Kriyā Tantras, as well as the Pāramitā system, and the Sūtra and Abhidharma Piṭakas, along with other treatises;
The Jātakas and the Itivṛttakas, as well as the opinions of the authors of the hymns,
the entirety of the Vijñānavāda, and likewise that which is the Madhyamaka;
Having recollected the worldly treatises as well as the instructions transmitted through the succession of gurus, I have now been requested [to speak].
An exposition of its profound and vast unfolding is being composed with a mind moistened by compassion for sentient beings of dull intellect.

Now, the structural arrangement of this *Nāmasaṃgīti* is being explained. It is as follows: the request; the response; the survey of the six families; the sequence of awakening through the *māyājāla*; the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) by way of the illustrious Vajrasattva; the wisdom of the perfectly pure realm of phenomena (*suviśuddhadharmadhātujñāna*) in the nature of Mahāvairocana; the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) by way of Akṣobhya; the discerning wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*) through the gateway of Amitābha; and the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*) in the form of Ratnasaṃbhava.

The knowledge of the performance of duties through the nature of Amoghasiddhi; the praise of gnosis by way of the five Tathāgatas; the benefits; the arrangement of mantras; and the conclusion—these are the fourteen topics concerning the body.

Therein, beginning with “Then Vajradhara... and ending with “standing before him with body bowed,” there is the request made in sixteen verses. Then, beginning with “Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni... and ending with “It is well, Blessed One,” there is the reply in six verses. Then, beginning with “Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni [beheld] all... and ending with “the great family of the Great Uṣṇīṣa,” there is the survey of the six families in two verses.

Beginning with the verse "imāṃ ṣaṇmantra... and continuing up to "arapacanāya te namaḥ," the sequence of awakening through the *Māyājāla* is indicated by these three verses. Beginning with "tad yathā... and continuing up to "mahāyānanayottamaḥ," the nature of Bodhicittavajra is expressed by means of the great maṇḍala of the Vajradhātu through these fourteen verses.

Beginning with "Mahāvairocana Buddha" and ending with "Vajrāṅkuśa, the Great Noose," there is praise by means of twenty-four and a quarter verses through the nature of the *suviśuddhadharmadhātujñāna* (the wisdom of the perfectly pure realm of phenomena). Beginning with "Vajrabhairava, the Terrifying" and ending with "Ghoṣa, the Best among those who possess sound," there is praise by means of nine and three-quarter verses through the nature of the *ādarśajñāna* (mirror-like wisdom).

Beginning with "Suchness, reality, selflessness," and so forth, up to "the flame of gnosis, most radiant," there is praise by way of the door of discerning wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*) in forty-two verses. Beginning with "The supreme achiever of desired aims," and so forth, up to "the great jewel Ratnaketu," there is praise by way of the nature of the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*) in twenty-four verses.

Beginning with "The one to be awakened by all the perfectly awakened ones" and so forth, up to "Mañjuśrī, the best among the glorious," there is praise by means of the wisdom of accomplishing activities (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*) through fifteen verses. Beginning with "Homage to you, the giver of boons, O Vajra-tip" and so forth, up to "Ognosis-body, homage be to you," there is praise of the five wisdoms by way of the five Tathāgatas through five verses.

This is the praise of the benefits, beginning with "O Vajrapāṇi, O Vajradhara," and so forth, up to "the King of Dharma. The praise by way of mantra begins with "Oṃ sarvadharmā... and so forth, up to "...dharmadhātujñānagarbha Āḥ. Then, the concluding praise begins with "O Vajradhara," and so forth, up to "...taught by all the Perfect Buddhas."

Thus, in one place, the complete praise is contained within one hundred and sixty-two verses and a supplementary section of one hundred and fifty verses on the benefits. And this is the summary meaning of the *Nāmasaṃgīti* of the Blessed One, the Wisdom-Body of all Tathāgatas, Mañjuśrī-jñānasattva.

Since the activity of all people everywhere is preceded by a determination regarding the connection, the subject matter, the purpose, and the ultimate goal of that purpose—arising from doubt concerning the meaning of the sentence—the connection and so forth are the things to be expressed by this *Nāmasaṃgīti*.

For instance, if its connection and subject matter were not stated, then discerning persons—suspecting it to be incoherent and purposeless like the speech of a madman—would not proceed to listen; therefore, its connection and subject matter must necessarily be stated. However, those possessed of faith proceed simply on the authority of the Blessed One’s word; for them, the subject matter and so forth need not be stated, because their engagement proceeds from faith alone.

Therefore, what is to be expressed here is non-dual gnosis (*advayajñāna*). And so he will state [later] regarding the benefits: "Namely, for the sake of causing entry into the nature of non-duality, by means of the retention and illumination of the names. As for the expression, *nāmasaṃgīti*: "gāna" means singing; "gīti" means song; "saṃgīti" means perfect song. Thus, the perfect song of names is *nāmasaṃgīti*. The "names" are those found in the Yogatantra, Kriyātantra, Caryātantra, the scriptural discourses (*pravacana*), the Sūtras, the Abhidharma, the Vinaya, as well as worldly and transcendent [terms], and all things both stationary and moving.

The "concerted music" of those names exists only through a figurative convention and not from the perspective of ultimate reality; however, it does exist conventionally, according to the principle that "all this is merely name, up to the limit of the peak of existence. Between these two, there is a relationship characterized either as signifier and signified, or as means and goal.

And the purpose for Bodhisattvas who practice the way of mantra is the attainment of non-dual gnosis by those who, through both resolute conviction and mental engagement with reality, directly realize it by means of a supreme, unclouded faith that penetrates all phenomena and is permeated by wisdom. Furthermore, the ultimate state of the Tathāgata, which arises from the culmination of the excellence of cultivation, should be understood as the "purpose of the purpose."
Now, however, the meaning of the word (padārtha) is being explained.
Then the glorious Vajradhara, the supreme tamer of the difficult to tame, the hero who conquers the three worlds, the king of secrets, and the lord of the vajra— || 1 ||

The word *atha* refers to Vajradhara, because he has been introduced as the requester [of the teaching]. From the "Chapter on the Net of Samādhis" within the *Āryamāyājāla-ṣoḍaśasāhasrika-mahāyogatantra*, there is the *Paramārthanāmasaṃgīti* spoken by the Blessed One Śākyamuni concerning the Blessed Mañjuśrī-jñānasattva; for the purpose of requesting that [teaching], the Blessed Vajradhara spoke again with the word *atha* in order to favor sentient beings of dull faculties. Here, the word *atha* signifies immediate succession (*ānantarya*).

Now, the connection is as follows: Vajradhara, together with Bhṛkuṭītaraṅga and the others, having bowed to the Lord, the Buddha, the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, and standing before him with palms joined in reverence, spoke this. He is called Vajradhara because he "holds the vajra" (*vajraṃ dhārayati*). By this term, profundity (*gāmbhīrya*) is expressed. He is "the Glorious One" (*śrīmān*) because he possesses those goddesses who are Śrīs; by this, magnificence (*audārya*) is indicated. Consequently, what has been stated?
That the Blessed One Vajradhara is of the nature of wisdom and means (*prajñopāyātmaka*). For this very reason, it is said in the *Śrīsaṃvara*:

"In the expanse of all space is the Tathāgata Śrīvajrasattva. Those who are "difficult to tame" (*durdānta*) are the Īśvara and others who are subdued by suffering; he is their "tamer" (*damaka*) and instructor because he disciplines those such as the Īśvara through the Vajradhara. Because he is supreme, the Vajradhara is "the Other" (*para*). The three worlds are the *bhūrloka*, *bhuvarloka*, and *svarloka*. He whose nature it is to conquer these is the "Conqueror of the Three Worlds" (*trilokavijayī*). Alternatively, the three brothers—Jayakara, Madhukara, and Sarvārthasiddhikara—are the "three worlds. He whose nature it is to conquer them is the "Conqueror of the Three Worlds."

For this very reason, the Blessed Lord Vajradhara is a hero, because he cannot be overcome by spokes [of the wheel]. In the *Śrītattvasaṃgraha*, five secrets are recited; for it is said: "In whatever way sentient beings naturally come to be disciplined, in that very way one who is pure through passion and the rest should act for the benefit of sentient beings."
For the sake of the welfare of all beings, by means of the Buddha's teaching,
even while slaying all beings, he is not defiled by sin.
For the sake of the welfare of all beings, through the application of the Buddha-body...
But one who seizes the wealth of others is not tainted by sin.
There is no pleasure equal to passion; by receiving that from the Victors and serving the wives of others for the sake of sentient beings, one shall obtain merit.
"For the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings and for the cause of the Buddha's teaching,
one who performs all actions shall obtain great merit."

The king of those five secret ones is the Guhyarāja; or, he who rules by means of the secret ones is the Guhyarāja. The *kuliśa* is the *vajra*; its lord is the Kuliśeśvara. The Blessed One Vajradhara, having stood before him with palms joined in reverence (*kṛtāñjalipuṭa*), spoke these words that are about to be related. This verbal phrase is to be applied in every instance.
His eyes are like blossomed white lotuses, his face is like a fully opened lotus,
and he repeatedly brandishes an excellent vajra with his own hand.

"Vibuddha" means a white lotus (*puṇḍarīka*), which is a white water-lily; "vibuddham akṣi" means an eye that has blossomed or opened. Thus, the analysis of the compound is as follows: "vibuddhapuṇḍarīka" consists of "vibuddha" and "puṇḍarīka. He whose two eyes (*locane*) are like a blossomed white lotus is so described. [228] "Protphulla" means fully bloomed; "kamalam" means a lotus. "Prakarṣotphullakamalavad ānanam" refers to a face (*mukha*) that is like a lotus blooming to the highest degree. He whose face is thus is so described.

The connection [of the words] is as follows: having grasped the middle of the vajra with his own hand, and repeatedly receiving the vajra as it was thrown back again, he brandished it while saying this.
Accompanied by infinite Vajrapāṇis, foremost among whom were Bhṛkuṭītaraṅga and others—heroes who subdue the difficult-to-tame, possessing forms that are both heroic and loathsome. || 3 ||

In the *Śrīvajrapāṇyabhiṣeka-tantra*, five hundred hosts of wrathful deities (*krodhagaṇa*), headed by Bhṛkuṭītaraṅga, are recited as the attendants of the illustrious Vajradhara. It should be understood that the Lord Vajradhara, together with half of them, bowed down to the Perfectly Awakened One and spoke this. And those hosts of wrathful deities are, in the ultimate sense, infinite; therefore it says, "by the infinite Vajrapāṇis. They too, like Vajradhara, are tamers of the difficult-to-tame; for this very reason it says, "by the tamers of the difficult-to-tame. For this very reason, they are heroes (*vīra*).

Because they cannot be overcome by them, he says "by the heroes" (*vīraiḥ*). Of what flavor? Of the flavor of heroism (*vīrarasa*). Of what form? Of the form of the loathsome (*bībhatsarūpin*). For this very reason, it says "by those having the forms of the heroic and the loathsome.
[Verse 4: With their own hands brandishing the tips of flashing vajras, they are supreme in performing the welfare of the world through wisdom, skillful means, and great compassion.

"By those tossing upwards" means by those lifting [them] high. By what? By their own hands. "With the tips of flashing vajras" means those whose tips—the front parts—of the vajras are flashing; they are "those with flashing vajra-tips. Of what nature are they? They are "those whose nature is to effect the welfare of the world through wisdom, skillful means, and great compassion," that is, *prajñopāyamahākaruṇājagadarthakarāḥ*. In this context, wisdom (*prajñā*) is the discernment of all phenomena (*sarvadharmāṇāṃ pravicayaḥ*).

*Upāya* is the aspiration to accomplish the welfare of all sentient beings according to their spiritual capacity, by way of demonstrating the mundane and supramundane paths without exception. *Kam* means "what"; *ruṇaddhi* means "it obstructs. Thus, *karuṇā* (compassion) is so called because one who possesses compassion (*kāruṇika*), being pained by the suffering of others, obstructs his own happiness; hence it is *karuṇā*. This great compassion is *mahākaruṇā*, which has the nature of being without objective support (*anālambanātmikā*). *Jagat* and *jagat* and *jagat*—these *jaganti* are the three realms (*traidhātuka*).

Their purpose is their objective; therefore, he says: "by those who perform the welfare of the world through wisdom, skillful means, and great compassion. For this very reason, those wrathful ones are supreme and excellent; thus, he says: "by the supreme ones."

Together with the Protectors who perform the deeds of a Buddha, who possess joyful and contented intentions, who are delighted, and who manifest forms of wrathful bodies, all with their bodies bowed in prostration. || 5 ||

What is their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)? Their intrinsic nature is one of joyful and contented intention (*āśaya*). In this context, "joyful" refers to the body, and "contented" refers to the mind. "Intention" (*āśaya*) means purpose (*abhiprāya*). Therefore, the meaning is as follows: those whose intentions are joyful and contented are "those of joyful and contented intention"; thus it says, "by those of joyful and contented intention. For this very reason, they are "glad" (*muditā*), meaning delighted, because of performing the welfare of all sentient beings; for this very reason it says, "by those who are glad" (*muditaiḥ*). The form of a manifestation (*vigraha*) is "manifestation-form" (*vigraharūpa*); the manifestation-form of the wrathful ones (*krodha*) is "wrathful manifestation-form" (*krodhavigraharūpa*).

What is that form? It consists of the great and terrifying *aṭṭahāsa* laughter, multiple heads, hands, and feet, distorted eyes, upward-pointing hair, tawny eyebrows, ornaments of garlands of skulls, snake-jewels, a tiger-skin garment, and so forth. Those who possess such [forms] are "those whose bodies have the form of wrath" (*krodhavigraharūpiṇaḥ*). Therefore, it says: "by those whose bodies have the form of wrath. The "deeds of the Buddhas" (*buddhakṛtyāni*) are the tasks (*kṛtyāni*) to be performed. Therefore, it says: "by those who perform the deeds of the Buddhas."

Therefore, because they perform the activities of a Buddha, they are protectors (nātha) and teachers; thus, it says "by the protectors. Those whose bodies are bowed are "those with bowed bodies" (praṇatavigraha). Thus, [the connection is: together with those who have bowed bodies, the Blessed One Vajradhara spoke this which is about to be described.
Having prostrated before the Lord, the Perfectly Awakened One, the Blessed Tathāgata,
he stood before him with palms joined in reverence and spoke these words.

Having done what? Having prostrated. To whom? To the Lord (*nātha*). Why is he called the Lord? Because he instructs the world of those who are without a protector, he is the Lord, the Master; to him. Furthermore, how qualified is this Lord? He says: "the Fully Awakened One" (*saṃbuddha*), meaning the Perfectly Enlightened One (*samyaksaṃbuddha*), not a disciple (*śrāvaka*) or a solitary buddha (*pratyekabuddha*). Again, he further qualifies the Lord as "the Blessed One" (*bhagavant*); he is the Blessed One because he is endowed with glory (*bhaga*), or because of his destruction of the four Māras. And thus it has been said: "Afflictions, karma, and likewise birth, as well as the obscurations of affliction and the knowable."
"Because he has shattered all opposing factors, he is remembered here as the Blessed One (Bhagavān). Thus it is said.

By this etymological method, he is called the Blessed One (*bhagavān*) because he has destroyed the afflictions (*kleśa*) and so forth; or alternatively, because of his possession of qualities such as sovereignty (*aiśvarya*). Thus it is said: "Sovereignty, wealth, beauty, fame, glory, knowledge, and effort—of these six, the word *bhaga* is the traditional designation."

Furthermore, he asks what kind of Protector [he is], and says: "the Tathāgata. One who has gone (*gata*) to suchness (*tathatā*), which is emptiness (*śūnyatā*), is a Tathāgata. Alternatively, one who goes in the same manner as those Tathāgatas have gone, go, and will go is a Tathāgata. "Having bowed to that Tathāgata" connects with the preceding [verse]. Standing before him with palms joined in reverence, the Blessed Lord Vajradhara said this.
For my benefit, for my sake, and out of compassion for me, O Lord, [teach] so that I may become a possessor of the perfect awakening through the Net of Illusion. (7)

"maddhitāya" and so forth. "maddhitaṃ" means what is beneficial for me; it is beneficial because it is wholesome for the future, as it pertains to the welfare of subsequent lives. "mamārthāya" means for my purpose; "me" means for me. O Lord, "anukampāya" means for the sake of your compassion, that is, for the sake of your grace, "yathā" meaning in such a manner that I may become a recipient. Of what? He says: "of the realization of the Net of Illusion" (*māyājālābhisaṃbodheḥ*). The "realization of the Net of Illusion" is the name of the sequence [of practice]; the connection is with the verbal action to be mentioned later: "may the Blessed One reveal it in such a way that I may become a recipient of it. [234]
For the benefit of all sentient beings who are submerged in the mire of ignorance and whose minds are agitated by the afflictions, and for the attainment of the unsurpassed fruit. (8)

And for the benefit of all sentient beings who are submerged in the mire of ignorance. Here, "ignorance" is *avidyā*; because it is a place where one becomes stuck and because it is difficult to cross over, it is like a mire, and thus called "mire. For the benefit of those sentient beings who are submerged therein. Furthermore, he describes what those sentient beings are like: "those whose minds are agitated by the afflictions. There are six afflictions (*kleśas*). As it is said in the Abhidharma: "Pride, views, doubt, attachment, aversion, and delusion."

Those beings whose minds are agitated by those afflictions are "those whose minds are agitated by afflictions. Therefore, for their sake—that is, for the attainment of that [state]—it is said: "May the Blessed One reveal [the path] for the attainment of the unsurpassed fruit."

May the Fully Awakened One, the Blessed One, the Teacher, the Guru of the World— supreme knower of the reality of the Great Samaya and master who understands the dispositions of the faculties— reveal [this].

"May the Blessed One reveal it," he said. "The Fully Awakened One" (*saṃbuddha*) is by way of the gate of Śāśvata (the Eternal). "The Teacher" (*śāstṛ*) is by way of the gate of Akṣobhya, because of his instruction of the world. "The Teacher of the World" (*jagadguru*) is by way of the gate of Ratnasaṃbhava. The Blessed One is the Lord of the Pledge (*samaya*), the glorious Vajrasattva. He is both great and a pledge, thus "Great Pledge" (*mahāsamaya*). His reality is the "Reality of the Great Pledge" (*mahāsamayatattva*). One who knows that is the "Knower of the Reality of the Great Pledge" (*mahāsamayatattvajña*); this is by way of the gate of Amitābha.

The faculties are weak, middling, or superior; their disposition (*āśaya*) is their intention (*abhiprāya*). He who knows that is "the knower of the disposition of the faculties" (*indriyāśayavid*), by way of Amoghasiddhi. Thus, the meaning is: may the Blessed One, who is identical with the five Tathāgatas, the supreme and most excellent, reveal [this].
O Blessed One, [I bow] to the one who is the body of gnosis, the Great Uṣṇīṣa, the Lord of Speech, the Gnosis-being Mañjuśrī, the embodiment of wisdom, the Self-arisen One. || 10 ||

Now, regarding the passage beginning with "O Blessed One, of the Jñānakāya," and so forth: the connection is with the verbal action to be stated later, namely, "O Blessed One, I shall uphold that *Nāmasaṃgīti* which belongs to the Mañjuśrījñānasattva. Of what kind is this Jñānakāya? It is the "Jñānakāya" because knowledge itself is the body; thus, it is "of the Jñānakāya" by way of the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*). Furthermore, it is "of the Mahoṣṇīṣa."

"Of the Great Uṣṇīṣa" means he who possesses a great uṣṇīṣa; "of that Great Uṣṇīṣa" refers to him by way of the door of the knowledge of equality (*samatājñāna*). His state of being the Great Uṣṇīṣa is due to his consisting of the consecration of all Tathāgatas. "Of the Lord of Speech" (*gīṣpati*): speech (*gir*) refers to sounds; their lord or master is the Lord of Speech (*gīṣpati*); "of that Lord of Speech" refers to him by way of the door of the knowledge of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*). "Of the Embodiment of Knowledge": knowledge itself is the embodiment, thus "the Embodiment of Knowledge" (*jñānamūrti*); "of that Embodiment of Knowledge" refers to him by way of the door of the knowledge of accomplishing activities (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*).

Regarding the term *svayaṃbhuvaḥ*: he is called *svayaṃbhū* because he exists by himself; the meaning is that he exists through the power of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*). Thus it is said in the *Śrīparamādya*:
"The gnosis of Samantabhadra will be realized by itself."

Therefore, the term "of that Self-Existent One" (*svayaṃbhū*) refers to the gateway of the knowledge of the perfectly pure *dharmadhātu*. What is being stated? The Blessed One Mañjuśrī-jñānasattva consists of the five knowledges. He is Mañjuśrī because his splendor (*śrī*) is gentle (*mañju*). He is called a "knowledge-being" (*jñānasattva*) because he dwells in the heart of all Tathāgatas. Thus, he is Mañjuśrī-jñānasattva, being both Mañjuśrī and a knowledge-being.

This is not a bodhisattva who is a lord of the ten stages; rather, it is non-dual gnosis, the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), which is itself Mañjuśrī, the Knowledge-Being (jñānasattva). For this very reason, the venerable Dignāga said:
"The perfection of wisdom is non-dual gnosis; that is the Tathāgata."

"I shall uphold that *Nāmasaṃgīti* belonging to that Mañjuśrī-jñānasattva, who consists of the five wisdoms. "The *Nāmasaṃgīti*, which is supreme—profound in meaning, vast in meaning, of great meaning, peerless, auspicious, and virtuous in the beginning, middle, and end. (11)

To the question "Of what kind? he says: "Of profound meaning," and so forth. That which is profound and is also a meaning is "profound meaning" (*gambhīrārtha*), namely the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatārtha*). That in which this exists is "of profound meaning. Therefore, [the thought is]: "I shall uphold that. "Of sublime meaning" (*udārārthā*): that which is sublime and is also a meaning is "sublime meaning" (*udārārtha*), which is to say the meaning of the Vaipulya. That in which this is found is "of sublime meaning," and that [he shall uphold]. "Of great meaning" (*mahārthā*): that in which there is a great meaning is "of great meaning."

Furthermore, its "great purpose" (*mahārthatva*) consists in the welfare of all sentient beings without exception, because it fulfills every [need]. "Unequaled" (*asamā*): that which has no equal is "unequaled. Why is it unequaled? Because its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is the *dharmadhātu*. "Auspicious" (*śivā*): because it is the pacification of all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). "Virtuous in the beginning, middle, and end": it is virtuous in three ways because one attains joy, gladness, and pliancy during the stages of hearing, reflecting, and meditating. That [Perfection of Wisdom], I shall uphold.
"The supreme Nāmasaṃgīti" has its meaning already explained.
That which was spoken by the Buddhas of the past, which those of the future will speak, and which the perfectly awakened ones of the present speak again and again—[that is this]. (12)
And that which is fully proclaimed in this *Māyājāla-mahātantra* by the immeasurable, joyful holders of mantra, the Great Vajradharas; (13)
"And I, with firm resolve, shall uphold this until final liberation.

(14ab) Again, he asks what its specific characteristics are, and says: "By those of the past," and so forth. For that *Nāmasaṃgīti* which was spoken by the Buddhas of the past, which those who are the future perfectly enlightened ones will speak, and which the present Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, speak again and again—[239] "and the perfectly enlightened ones of the present speak it repeatedly."
"Regarding the passage beginning with *māyājāla* and so forth: that which is joyfully sung in this *Māyājāla-mahātantra* by immeasurable Great Vajradharas who are holders of the great mantras—"

And I shall uphold this until final departure, as far as nirvāṇa. Of what nature is one of firm intention? One whose intention—that is, whose resolve—is firm and unshakable is "one of firm intention."

This is what is meant: the *Nāmasaṃgīti* is that which has been spoken by the Tathāgatas existing throughout the three times; therefore, it demonstrates the equality of this Dharma-discourse with space. Thus it is said:
"Whether Tathāgatas arise or do not arise, this true nature (*dharmatā*) of phenomena remains constant"—this is what is being shown.
"Just as I may become, O Lord, the holder of the secrets of all the perfectly awakened ones...

(14cd). "Just as I may become," and so forth: "O Lord, just as I may become the holder of the secrets of all the perfectly awakened ones, so may you reveal [them]"—this is the connection with what precedes. *Dhṛg* is the correct reading.
"I shall reveal [the teachings] to sentient beings according to the particularities of their inclinations" (15ab).

Having realized that [truth] exactly as it is, I shall reveal it to all sentient beings according to the particularities of their individual inclinations. To the question "For what purpose?", he says:
"For the destruction of all afflictions without exception, and for the abandonment of all ignorance without exception. (15cd)

In this context, "all afflictions" refers to the primary and secondary afflictions (*kleśa-upakleśa*), for their destruction. "For the abandonment of all ignorance" means that ignorance regarding all objects of knowledge is "all ignorance," and for the sake of the abandonment of that all ignorance, I shall reveal [this teaching].
Having thus entreated the Tathāgata, Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of Secrets, stood before him with his body bowed low and his hands joined in the gesture of reverence. (16)

"Thus," and so forth. In this manner, the Blessed One Guhyendra Vajrapāṇi, having made a request to the Tathāgata—where "Guhyendra" refers to the lord or king of the *guhya* (secret) yakṣas who dwell in Aḍakavatī—he stands before him with palms joined, his body bowed and inclined. "Request" (*adhyeṣaṇā*) is a petition preceded by formal preparation; here, that preparation consists of prostration and the like.
In the *Āryanāmasaṃgītiṭīkā*, titled *Nāmamantrārthāvalokinī*, the first chapter on the Request concludes.
[241] Chapter 2: Now, the Blessed One Śākyamuni, the Perfectly Awakened One, the Supreme among Men...
Having extended his own auspicious tongue from his mouth, long and broad.

Immediately following the request, he gives the reply beginning with "Then Śākyamuni," and so forth. He is the Sage (*muni*) of the Śākya clan because of his engagement in the silence (*mauna*) of body, speech, and mind. The term "Blessed One, the Perfectly Awakened One" has its meaning already explained. "Supreme among bipeds" means that bipeds are gods and humans; he is the supreme, the most excellent among them.

Having extended and withdrawn his own tongue from his mouth—meaning from his own mouth—he [uttered] that which was long (*āyatām*), extensive (*sphītām*), very thick (*bahalatarām*), and beautiful (*śubhām*), resembling a right-spiraling conch shell, and which is the abode of all phenomena (*sarvadharmālayām*).
Displaying a smile that purifies the three lower realms for all beings, illuminating the three worlds, and subduing the enemy of the four Māras. (18)

Having done what? [The text says] "having displayed a smile," and so forth. The connection is as follows: having displayed a smile—which purifies the three lower realms (*apāya*) of beings, namely the purification of the hells, animals, and hungry ghosts—he addressed Vajrapāṇi. There are three signs for the Dharma teaching of the Tathāgatas, namely: a smile, a glance, and the stimulation by light rays. In some cases there is one, in some two, and in some all three occur simultaneously.

For example, in the *Śrī-māyājāla-tantra*, two are taught: the smile and the gaze. In some places, three are mentioned, as in the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā*: the gaze of Maitreya, the smile, and the radiation of light rays from the mouth. In other places, only one is mentioned, as here in this very *Nāmasaṃgīti*: "having displayed a smile for the worlds. And that smile is of four kinds.

[This occurs] through the radiation from the limbs and minor members, the radiation from the pores of the skin, the radiation of the natural radiance, and the radiation of rays from the faculty of the tongue. Thus, herein lies the miracle of the tongue (*jihvā-prātihārya*), which is the prior sign of the teaching. By the words "making the three worlds manifest" and so forth, he shows that after displaying a smile—which makes manifest and illuminates the three worlds, namely *bhūr*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svar*—he addressed Vajrapāṇi; such is the connection.

Furthermore, as to what kind of smile it was, he says: "the instruction of the enemy of the four Māras. The four Māras are the Māras of the aggregates (skandha), afflictions (kleśa), death (mṛtyu), and the son of a god (devaputra). These very ones are the enemies; their instruction is the teaching and the subjugation of them.
With a sweet, Brahma-like voice that filled the three worlds,
he addressed Vajrapāṇi, the lord of secrets and possessor of great power.

Having displayed a smile that filled the three worlds, he addressed Vajrapāṇi with words and speech. Of what nature was it? It was sweet, for sweetness consists in being pleasant to the ear; it was "Brahmic" (*brāhmī*), because it was endowed with the voice of Brahmā. Regarding the "voice of Brahmā," the word *brahma* is a designation for that which is great and possesses great qualities, as it has been said:
"It produces Brahmic merit within an assembly of many thousands."
By the word "thousandfold" (sāhasra), the trichiliocosm (trisāhasramahāsāhasra) world-system is to be understood; the meaning is "in an assembly consisting of many thousands. And as it has been said:
"He pervades the trichiliocosm world-system with his voice," such that those on the outside hear just as those on the inside do.

In this context, those who reside within this triple-thousand great-thousandfold world system are the "internal" ones; those separated by other world systems are the "external" ones. Because of its greatness, it is called *brahma*; the voice of that [greatness] is the "Brahma-voice."
Alternatively, the Blessed One Śākyamuni is Brahmā. This is his *brāhmī* speech. With that single *brāhmī* voice, filling and pervading the three worlds, he addressed Vajrapāṇi. As it has been said:

"Even though the speech of the Destroyer of Existence is but one, through various designations distinct for each region, it becomes the cause for the awakening of all people, being unerring and clearly articulated."
Excellent, O glorious Vajradhara! Excellent to you, O Vajrapāṇi, since you, endowed with great compassion, act for the sake of the welfare of the world. (20)
You are prepared to hear from me the *Nāmasaṃgīti*, which is of great significance, purifying, and the destroyer of evil, belonging to Mañjuśrī, the Wisdom Body. (21)
"Therefore, O Lord of Guhyakas, I shall teach it well to you.

(22ab) "Excellent, O Vajradhara," and so forth. "Excellent" means for you, Vajrapāṇi. "O glorious Vajradhara, since you are prepared to hear from me that *Nāmasaṃgīti* which pertains to the Wisdom-Body (*jñānakāya*) of Mañjuśrī, therefore, O Lord of Guhyakas, I shall teach it well to you"—this is the connection. For what purpose have you questioned me? "For the sake of the welfare of the world," meaning, being endowed with great compassion, for the benefit of the world.
Of what kind is the *Nāmasaṃgīti* that he is intent on hearing? It is "purifying," meaning auspicious; it is "the destroyer of evil," meaning the destroyer of sin.

"Listen with a one-pointed mind; very well, Blessed One," [he said]. Regarding "listen with a one-pointed mind," this implies: do not listen like a jar with its opening turned downward or filled with impurities; rather, listen well. When the Blessed One had spoken thus, Vajradhara replied, "Blessed Śākyamuni, let it be so. He meant that he would listen according to the very sequence just described.
In the *Āryanāmasaṃgītiṭīkā*, titled *Nāmamantrārthāvalokinī*, the second chapter, "The Response," consisting of six verses, is concluded.
[246] Chapter 3: Now, the Blessed One Śākyamuni [addressed] the entire great family of mantras.
Having surveyed the family of the mantra-vidyādhara and the three families. || 23 ||

Now, regarding the observation of the six families (*ṣaṭkula*), he speaks another response: "Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni [spoke] this summary statement, 'The entire great family of mantra. Having observed that, he spoke this verse concerning the non-arising nature (*anutpādadharmiṇī*) belonging to Mañjuśrījñānasattva, the Lord of Speech. This is connected with the verbal action to be described hereafter.

Regarding "the family of the mantra-vidyādhara": one who holds (dhārayati) knowledge (vidyā) is a vidyādhara. That which is of the nature of mantra and is a vidyādhara is a mantra-vidyādhara; it is not of the nature of a dhāraṇī. Its family is the mantra-vidyādhara-kula, meaning the karma-kula. "The three families" refers to the Vairocana family because its intrinsic nature consists of body, speech, and mind. [247] The great worldly and transcendent family, the family that illuminates the world, The supreme Mahāmudrā family, and the great Mahoṣṇīṣa family. (24)

Regarding the phrase "the worldly and supramundane family" (*lokalokottarakula*): the root *lok* means "to see. That which is seen is the world (*loka*). Its family is the worldly-supramundane family; this means the Lotus Family (*padmakula*).

"Great is the family of Lokāloka. Lokāloka means the illumination of the worlds; [it refers to] Akṣobhya, because his nature is the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*). His family is the Lokāloka-family, which is indeed the supreme Vajra-family, because Vairocana and the others have the nature of bodhicitta. His family is the Mahāmudrā-family—this is the meaning. "Great is the family of Mahoṣṇīṣa. Because he bestows the consecration of the Dharma-kingdom over the triple world upon all the Tathāgatas, he possesses the state of Mahoṣṇīṣa.
His family is the Mahoṣṇīṣa-family, which is the great Ratna-family—this is the meaning.
The third chapter, the Survey of the Six Families, in the *Āryanāmasaṃgīti-ṭīkā Nāmamantrārthāvalokinī*.
[248] Chapter 4:

Now, the sequence of the awakening of the glorious *Māyājāla*, as transmitted through the lineage of gurus, is being explained. It is contained within the sixteen-thousand-verse *Śrīmāyājāla*. Therein, first of all, a bodhisattva who practices the conduct of the oral transmission of mantras and desires to directly realize this *Nāmasaṃgīti*—the crest-jewel of the Blessed One Mañjuśrī-jñānasattva, the gnosis-body of all Tathāgatas and the embodiment of gnosis, which is non-dual and the ultimate truth—and who possesses the intention to protect the entire realm of sentient beings without exception, [should act] toward sentient beings with material things...
Having gathered [these merits], one should generate the mind set upon unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*). And so it has been said:
"May all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas attend to me! I, named so-and-so, from this moment until I sit at the seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), generate the supreme, unsurpassed mind of enlightenment."
Just as the Protectors of the three times have made their resolve for perfect enlightenment,
so do I firmly undertake the threefold training in ethical discipline: the discipline of gathering virtuous qualities and the discipline of acting for the benefit of sentient beings.
From this day forward, I shall take up the vow born of the Buddha, the foremost among the Three Jewels— the unsurpassed Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha.
I accept the vajra, the bell, and the mudrā according to reality;
and I shall accept the master in the exalted assembly of the Great Vajra Family.
I shall bestow the fourfold gift six times every day,
at the auspicious and delightful time appropriate for the Great Jewel Family.
I receive the True Dharma— outer, secret, and belonging to the three vehicles—
within the pure Mahāpadma family, which gives birth to great awakening.
I truly undertake the vow associated with all [deities] in the exalted assembly of the Mahākarmakula, performing the rite of worship according to my ability.
Having generated the supreme, unsurpassed mind of awakening, and having undertaken the complete vow for the sake of all sentient beings:
"I shall ferry across those who have not crossed; I shall liberate those who are not liberated. [250]
"I shall bring comfort to beings who have not found comfort; I shall establish them in final peace."

Having first undertaken the vows and generated the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), one should meditate on the fivefold manifest enlightenment (*pañcākārābhisaṃbodhi*) by means of this sequence: first, one should meditate on the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) through the analogy of a reflection.

Just as various kinds of objects present at that particular place and time appear in a perfectly pure mirror-surface, so too, seeing the realms of sentient beings—distinguished by their various destinies, locations, and births—within the great bodhicitta which is the outflow of the utterly pure dharmadhātu, and beholding them there in the stainless mirror-like wisdom (ādarśajñāna), one should generate compassion directed toward those sentient beings.

"Alas! These beings are without a protector, without a refuge, without a resort, and suffering, submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra. For the sake of these beings, just as I shall liberate myself from all sufferings in every way, in every respect, and entirely, so too shall I liberate all beings"—thus one should perceive all beings within the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) without concealment.

Then, one should resolve upon the knowledge of equality through the yoga of the equality of the selflessness of all phenomena. Having contemplated that just as all phenomena are empty and without self, so too am I empty and without self, one should enter into the selflessness of all phenomena. And thus it is said: "As he understands himself, so he understands all sentient beings; as he understands all sentient beings, so he understands all phenomena," and so forth.
Then, through the realization of the intrinsic nature of the selflessness of all phenomena, one should generate compassion directed toward phenomena by means of the knowledge of equality.

Thereafter, the practitioner of mantra, having uttered the mantra— "The aspect is the gateway to all phenomena because they are primordially unarisen"— should meditate upon the meaning of the mantra both in its entirety and in brief.
Having contemplated the selflessness of phenomena together with non-objectification.
Such is the knowledge of analytical observation.

Immediately thereafter, one should cultivate the knowledge of the emptiness of the perfectly pure *dharmadhātu*, which is accompanied by great compassion that is itself without an object of reference, completely free from all grasped and grasper, luminous by nature, and devoid of the inherent existence of constituent parts. [252]

Then, the yogin who is devoid of the performance of activities for the benefit of all sentient beings—aroused by the power of the mental continuum established through previous vows—should cultivate the knowledge of the accomplishment of tasks (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*) by means of non-referential great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). Because this is a pure mundane knowledge (*śuddhalaukikajñāna*) obtained subsequent to non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpakajñāna*), the fulfillment of the welfare of all sentient beings is accomplished by that very [knowledge].

And that bodhicitta, characterized by the [great] resolve (*prasthāna*), should be understood as having the nature of both the conventional and the ultimate, and as a mind that is naturally purified (*prakṛtivaiyavadānika*).

Then the yogi, having discerned the mind as having the form of an illusion, situated in the region of space, naturally luminous, in the form of a star, and as the syllable *A*, should contemplate himself as Samantabhadra—arisen from that [mind], filled with garlands of blazing wrathful flames, blue in color, surrounded by many hundreds of thousands of rays, supreme bliss, and as the great syllable *HŪṂ*.

From that syllable *hūṃ*, rays of light of manifold forms stream forth; from the tips of those rays, all the Tathāgatas emerge. Those Tathāgatas go to all Buddha-fields and, having purified the realms of all sentient beings without exception in all world-systems, cause them to generate the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) and so forth, and display all the miraculous transformations of the Buddhas. One should visualize that they then return and re-enter into that *hūṃ* syllable.

One should meditate upon that [transformation] as the Wisdom-Vajra (*jñānavajra*), which possesses six colors beginning with blue, pervades the six Buddha-fields beginning with Abhirati, is garlanded with flames, is invincible to all Māras and enemies, has six faces, and five prongs. Having visualized a white syllable *Bhrūṃ* within the center of its vajra-pedestal, and having contemplated that it transforms into a stūpa made of the four jewels, equal in size to the triple-thousand great-thousandfold world system; within its interior, one should visualize the source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*) by means of the syllable *Hrīḥ*.
Above that, with the syllable *A*, one should visualize a double-vajra (*viśvavajra*), and by means of that, preside over a ground made of vajras and white in color.

Then, with the syllable *Bhṛūṃ*, one should contemplate a gabled palace (*kūṭāgāra*) with a peak-jewel of vajra-gems. As for its specific characteristics, he says: it is square, with four doors, and adorned with four archways (*toraṇa*).
Adorned with bells, cloth banners, flags, garlands, and yak-tail whisks.
And in all the corners, as well as at the junctions of the doors and the projections,
it is inlaid with vajra-jewels joined with half-moons.
One should delineate the outer mandala, adorned with various necklaces and half-necklaces, and embellished with powders of five colors.
Then, having entered its inner city which resembles a wheel,
one should place the second [city] known as Vajradhātu;
it is encircled by a garland of vajras and adorned with eight pillars.
And with the five dusts, it is adorned with necklaces, half-necklaces, and other ornaments.
Whatever characteristics have been described for the outer mandala,
one should perform all of them for this [inner mandala] as well, both in brief and in detail.
One should certainly not construct a single archway at the junctions of the doors;
therefore, one should not fashion archways for those doors.
Thereafter, one should arrange the seats for the deities in their proper order;
therein, in the center, one should indeed place the seat of the principal deity.
The knower of yoga should imagine the seats of Akṣobhya and the others in all directions, beginning with the east, as being fully accomplished from their respective seed-syllables.

Regarding the arrangement of the seats therein: in the center is the lion-throne (siṃhāsana), in the east the elephant-throne (gajāsana), in the south the horse-throne (turagāsana), in the west the peacock-throne (mayūrāsana), and in the north the garuḍa-throne (garuḍāsana).
One should visualize moon mandalas, which are fully perfected from the letter *A*, beginning with Sattvavajrī and extending as far as Vajrāveśa.

Then, upon the principal seat, there is Mahāvairocana, fully manifested from the syllable *Āḥ*. For that very mind, which by its very nature is devoid of the forms of subject and so forth, has the *dharmadhātu* as its intrinsic nature; it is four-faced because the *dharmadhātu*, as the object of focus for the four doors of liberation such as emptiness (*śūnyatā*), is the cause for the arising of all meditative absorptions (*samādhi*). It is white in color because its intrinsic nature is the *dharmadhātu*. It is endowed with a crown of matted hair and is without ornaments because his mind is peaceful.

Endowed with the *bodhyagrī* mudrā because his nature consists of wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*), one should resolve that one’s own self is that very Mahāvairocana. Through the yoga of the seats of the four Buddhas, there is a moon disc in his heart, and upon that, the Blessed One Ādibuddha, fully perfected from the syllable *dhīḥ*. He has five faces, meaning five mouths; he has five topknots, meaning five tufts of hair; because they are bound together, he has a crest of five tufts of hair. He is endowed with five colors.

One should meditate on [the deity] as blue in the east, yellow in the south, red in the west, and green in the north; with a white face situated at the crown of the head like that of a supreme horse-faced [deity]. He is peaceful, adorned with the ornaments of a youth, possessing amorous grace (*śṛṅgāra*), and clothed in variegated garments. Having eight arms, he holds the *Śatasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā*—divided into four parts—in his four hands against his heart.
With the other four hands, he holds the sword of wisdom (*prajñākhaḍga*) in the gesture of striking. One should visualize him established in the manner of the seats of the four Buddhas.
He spoke this verse of the Lord of Speech, which is joined with these six kings of mantras, which arises as non-duality, and whose nature is non-arising. (25)

The connection [of the sentence] is that the Lord of Speech (Brahmā) spoke this verse characterized by the twelve stages of the Tathāgatas. Of what nature is it? It is "endowed with the six mantra-kings," meaning it is possessed of the six mantras that are about to be described. What is its essence? It is "the arising of non-duality" (*advayodaya*). "Duality" refers to the grasped object (*grāhya*) and the grasping subject (*grāhaka*). That which does not possess these two is "non-dual" (*advaya*). "Arising" (*udaya*) means that from which something emerges. The "arising of non-duality" is *advayodaya*.

He spoke that verse in which non-duality arises. Furthermore, what is its specific characteristic? "Having the nature of non-arising" (anutpādadharmiṇīm); this means having the nature of the *dharmadhātu*, that is, having the nature of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
A Ā I Ī U Ū E AI O AU AṂ AḤ, abiding in the heart;
I am the Buddha, the embodiment of gnosis, of the Buddhas existing in the three times. [257] 26.
In the *Śrīvajramaṇḍālaṃkāra-tantra*, the stages of the twelve Tathāgatas are recited.
The great stage Samantaprabhā is like the orb of the sun;
the second, Amṛtaprabhā, is brilliantly radiant like the moon.
The third is Gaganaprabhā, which is established upon the ground of space;
the fourth ground is Vajraprabhā, which is delightful.
Through the application of firm resolve, it is conceived as a "vajra";
the fifth, named Ratnaprabhā, is established in the consecration.
The sixth is named Padmaprabhā; she shines brilliantly like a lotus.
Because her nature is the pure dharma, she is stainless and free from grasping.
The seventh is named Karmaprabhā, known as the performer of the Buddha's deeds;
the eighth is named Anupamā, for which no comparison exists.
The ninth is named Nirupamā (the Peerless), because it penetrates all points of comparison;
the tenth is the unsurpassed Buddha-stage, named Prajñāprabhā (the Radiance of Wisdom).
"The eleventh is the great ground of omniscience, radiant;
the twelfth is to be personally realized, fulfilling the knowledge of yogins. Thus it is said.
These twelve stages of the Tathāgatas should be understood as being fully established by the twelve vowels beginning with *a*.

"Of the Buddhas residing in the three times" refers to the Buddhas of the past and the future. "I am situated in the heart" is because I dwell in the hearts of all Tathāgatas. "The embodiment of gnosis" is because my nature is that of the gnosis-body (*jñānakāya*). "Buddha" is because of the awakening to things as they truly exist.
Oṃ, homage to you, O Vajratīkṣṇa, who cuts through suffering, whose form is the wisdom-knowledge, the Jñānakāya, the Lord of Speech, Arapacana. || 27 ||

Now, one should contemplate the wheel of wisdom (*prajñācakra*) within the heart of that Ādibuddha. Of what nature is it? He says: it indicates the meaning of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). And so it has been said:
"The hub is supported by the spokes, and the spokes are established upon the hub;
through the connection of dependent origination, this wheel revolves."

The [maṇḍala] is fully perfected by means of the syllable *A*, endowed with six colors, possessing six essences (*sāra*), joined with four girdles (*mekhalā*), and having a well-proportioned navel. Having meditated upon the syllable *A* in the center of its navel, one should visualize the mantras of the Blessed One Jñānasattva, beginning with the root mantra, as being white in color within the four girdles. Therein, on the first girdle: *Oṃ sarvadharmābhāvasvabhāvaviśuddhavajra a ā aṃ aḥ*.

On its second girdle, one should contemplate the twelve vowels which designate the stages (*bhūmi*) of the twelve Tathāgatas. Then, beginning from the first spoke, one should perform the placement of the six mantras according to the sequence of the family colors as follows: on the first, *oṃ vajratīkṣṇāya namaḥ*; on the second, *oṃ duḥkhacchedāya namaḥ*; on the third, *oṃ prajñājñānamūrtaye namaḥ*; on the fourth, *oṃ jñānakāyāya namaḥ*.

In the fifth [petal], *oṃ vāgīśvarāya namaḥ*. In the sixth: *oṃ arapacanāya namaḥ*. On the outer rim of the wheel, one should place the garland mantra (*mālāmantra*) of the Blessed One, the Wisdom-Body of all Tathāgatas: *aḥ āḥ sarvatathāgatahṛdaya hara hara oṃ hūṃ hrīḥ bhagavan jñānamūrte vāgīśvara mahāvāca sarvadharmagaganāmalasupariśuddhadharmadhātujñānagarbha āḥ*.
On the second outer girdle, one should place the letters beginning with *ka* and ending with *ha*. This is the arrangement of the mantras for the wheel. [260]

Having visualized oneself as the Lord Jñānasattva, who resides in the center of that wheel, born from the syllable *A*, possessing six faces, with the luster of the autumn moon, wearing excellent robes of sapphire-blue, with a halo of light having the brilliance of the orb of the rising sun, adorned with ornaments consisting of all the Tathāgatas, absorbed in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), seated upon a variegated lotus throne, holding two volumes of the Prajñāpāramitā atop blue utpala lotuses grasped in both hands, and endowed with the sentiment of tranquility (*śāntarasa*).

Having visualized a moon disc in his heart, one should place upon it the letter *A*, which is the nature of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), the cause for the arising of the knowledge of the omniscient one, the source of birth for all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, the basis for the accumulation of merit and knowledge for all great bodhisattvas, the ultimate syllable, and the cause of all syllables.

Then, one should visualize the mantra-syllables situated upon the wheel, endowed with their prescribed colors, well-distinguished, capable of shattering the mountain of ignorance, and radiant; and by means of those rays, one should contemplate one's own body as being illuminated. [261]

Illuminating [all things], rays of light issued forth from his four faces and, having pervaded the Sahā world-system, six-colored [rays] emerged from the six vajra-faces. Having gone to various buddha-fields throughout the entire expanse of space, they performed the welfare of the entire realm of sentient beings without exception in those buddha-fields. Then, having illuminated the assemblies of all the Tathāgatas, Buddhas, and Bodhisattvas, they entered through their mouths, circumambulated the vajra at their hearts, and [remained there].

Having drawn forth that wisdom-knowledge (prajñājñāna) through the equality of the selflessness of phenomena (dharmanairātmya), one should contemplate it as having entered through one's own mouths, becoming one with the mantra-syllables situated upon the moon in one's own heart, and remaining there.

Thus, the Bodhisattva who delights in uninterrupted cultivation and practices the conduct of the mantra-entrance, taking as his objective support the form of the Blessed One Mañjuśrī-jñānasattva—contemplating that form with the body of gnosis (*jñānakāya*), visualizing that form as the form of a moon disc, and meditating upon that form as the form of the syllable *A*—practicing in these three ways, shall before long behold that very [deity] in an emanated form-body (*nirmāṇarūpakāya*), by virtue of the power of discipline.

And one will behold all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas situated in the expanse of the sky, accompanied by their emanation-form bodies (*nirmāṇarūpakāya*). Then, through the power of cultivation, one attains Buddhahood and the state of Vajradhara in this very life; by this sequence, the stage of awakening according to the *Māyājāla* is indicated.

Now, six other wheels of wisdom (*prajñācakra*) are also described according to the distinction of families (*kulabheda*). In that regard, first, having performed the entire *ādiyoga*, one should draw forth the Blessed One Mahāvairocana who is situated in the center of his own maṇḍala; in his place, one should visualize Amitābha, red in color, born from the syllable *hrīḥ*, and established in meditative absorption (*samādhi*). Having likewise meditated upon the Ādibuddha in his heart, one should [visualize] an eight-spoked wheel endowed with four girdles in his heart, using the root mantra and so forth.

One should contemplate [the deity] surrounded [by a circle]. In the center of the hub of the wheel, one should visualize Vajratīkṣṇa, red in color, adorned with the ornaments of a youth, wearing a crest of five locks of hair, and clothed in variegated garments; he is the transformation of the syllable *hrīḥ*, holding a lotus in his left hand and a sword of wisdom (*prajñākhaḍga*) in his right hand. Having visualized him thus, one should meditate by generating the syllable *hrīḥ* upon a moon disc at his heart as before, and performing the process of emanation and reabsorption as previously described. Thus one should practice the meditation.

Again, having likewise meditated upon Akṣobhya in the center of the maṇḍala—blue in color, born from the syllable *HŪṂ*, and endowed with the earth-touching mudrā—and having visualized the Ādibuddha within his heart as well as an eight-spoked wheel in the same manner, one should perform the placement of mantras as before. Having placed the eight seed-syllables in the spokes, starting with *OṂ DUḤKHACCHEDĀYA NAMAḤ*, one should visualize in the center the Blessed One Vajrakhaḍga, arisen from the syllable *HŪṂ*, blue in color, in the form of a youth, adorned with all the ornaments of a child, and wearing five locks of hair.

Having visualized [the deity] wearing a silk garment (cīnapaṭṭa), holding a vajra in the left hand and a sword in the right, and having meditated on the syllable *hūṃ* upon a moon disc in his heart, one should perform the radiation and other rites in the same manner.

Again, in the same manner, one should visualize Vairocana in the center, white in color, joined with the bodhyagrī mudrā, and fully arisen from the syllable *Āḥ*. In his heart, one should likewise place the Ādibuddha, having formed a ten-spoked wheel interwoven with mantras. Having assigned the seed-syllables—*Oṃ prajñājñānamūrtaye namaḥ*—to the ten spokes, one should visualize the Blessed One Prajñājñāna in the center of the wheel, white in color, wearing five turbans, adorned with the ornaments of a youth, and clad in variegated garments, holding [in his left hand].

Having visualized a wheel-holder in the right hand and a sword of wisdom transformed from the syllable ĀḤ, one should meditate on a moon in its heart and the syllable ĀḤ above it, and perform the radiation and so forth in the same manner.

In the same way, having visualized Amoghasiddhi in the center of the mandala, green in color, endowed with the gesture of fearlessness (abhayamudrā), arisen from the seed-syllable *Aḥ*, and having likewise contemplated the Ādibuddha at his heart, one should fashion an eight-spoked wheel as before, interwoven with the mantra and so forth.

Then, having placed the eight seed-syllables—*oṃ jñānakāyāya namaḥ*—upon the eight spokes, one should visualize the Lord Jñānakāya in the center of the wheel: green in color, adorned with the ornaments of a youth, with a crest of five locks of hair, produced from the syllable *aḥ*, holding a crossed vajra in his left hand and a sword in his right; having meditated on a moon in his heart and the syllable *aḥ* above it, one should practice the meditation while performing the emission and reabsorption [of light] in that same manner.

Again, in the same manner, having meditated upon Ratnasaṃbhava in the center of the maṇḍala—yellow in color, endowed with the boon-granting gesture (varadamudrā), and arisen from the root syllable—one should likewise meditate upon Ādibuddha at his heart. Then, having placed an eight-spoked wheel joined with the root mantra and so forth, and having assigned the seed-syllables "Oṃ vāgiśvarāya namaḥ" to its eight spokes, one should [meditate upon] Vāgīśvara in the nave of the wheel: yellow in color, adorned with all ornaments, wearing five turbans and various garments, born from the seed-syllable Oṃ, and with his left [hand].

Having visualized [the deity] holding a jewel in his right hand and holding the sword of wisdom, one should contemplate the syllable Oṃ upon a moon disc in his heart and perform the emanation and so forth in that same manner.

In the same way, one should visualize in the center of the mandala the Bodhicittavajra, white in color, endowed with the sentiment of passion (*śṛṅgārarasa*), wearing a crown of the five Buddhas, seated in the pride of the vajra, adorned with all ornaments, holding a vajra and bell, and fully perfected by the syllable *A*. Having visualized him thus, one should likewise meditate upon the Lord Ādibuddha in his heart; and in his heart, a nine-spoked wheel inscribed with the root mantra and so forth, having placed the nine seed-syllables—*oṃ arapacanāya namaḥ*—upon the spokes.

Having visualized the Blessed One Arapacana at the hub of the wheel—white in color, adorned with the ornaments of a youth, wearing five locks of hair and variegated garments, arisen from the syllable *A*, marked by a book, and holding a sword in his hand—one should meditate on the syllable *A* above the moon at his heart; then, having performed the radiation, reabsorption, abiding, and stabilization as before, one should practice meditation. This application should be understood to apply everywhere.

This sequence of the glorious *Māyājāla-abhisambodhi* should also be understood as sixfold according to the divisions of the families (*kula*). For this very reason, there are seven wheels (*cakra*) in the *Ārya-nāmasaṃgīti*, and these are to be understood through the oral instructions of the Guru. Such is the extent of the sequence of the *Māyājāla-abhisambodhi*.
In the Commentary on the *Ārya-nāmasaṃgīti*, titled *The Illumination of the Meaning of the Name-Mantras*, the fourth chapter: the sequence of awakening according to the *Māyājāla*. [Three verses.
Chapter Five:
Thus, the Blessed One, the Buddha, the Perfectly Awakened One, is born from the syllable A.
The letter A is the foremost of all phonemes, of great significance, and the supreme syllable. || 28 ||

Now, he speaks of the radiation and so forth of the Vajra of Bodhicitta by way of the Great Maṇḍala of the Vajradhātu, beginning with the words "Thus, the Blessed One," and so on. "The Blessed One" refers to the Buddha; "the Perfectly Awakened One" has its meaning already explained. "Arisen from the letter A" means produced from the letter A, because the Blessed One, the Jñānasattva, has as his essential nature the perfectly pure Tathāgata-jñānakāya. Regarding that letter A which is upon the moon-maṇḍala in his heart, he now states its qualification: "the foremost of all colors."

The foremost existence (*agre-bhava*) is the preeminent among all castes and all syllables; it is preeminent and most excellent because it is their source (*tan-mukha*). "Of great purpose" (*mahārtha*) means that which is both great and an object (*artha*), thus "of great purpose"; its state of being of great purpose arises from its being the cause for establishing the welfare of the entire world. "Supreme syllable" (*paramākṣara*): by another synonym, it is called "syllable" (*akṣara*) because it does not perish (*na kṣarati*), since it is immovable in the form of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). It is "supreme" (*parama*) and it is "syllable" (*akṣara*), hence "supreme syllable. By this sequence, the description of the essential nature of the Gnosis-being (*jñānasattva*) and the syllable has been stated. [268]

Each one of those very [elements] should be contemplated by the yogins as being the nature of all the mandala deities arising from their own minds, insofar as they consist of the exclusion of all adverse factors (*vipakṣa*). Just as the [perfection of] emptiness is characterized as the door of liberation through its being the antidote to apprehension—because it indicates the non-apprehension of the distortions of one's own meditative absorptions—it is likewise, respectively, of the nature of the doors of liberation that are signless, wishless, and without volitional effort, by virtue of being the antidotes to signs, false aspirations, distortions, and formative activities (*abhisaṃskāra*).
Then, proceeding in sequence, with reference to the essential nature of the Mothers of the families beginning with Sattvavajrī, it is said:
The Great Vital Breath is indeed unarisen, devoid of verbal expression;
it is the supreme cause of all speech and is the perfect luminosity of all words. (29)

"Mahāprāṇa is indeed non-arising" refers to the intrinsic nature of Sattvavajrī; therein, "mahāprāṇa" is the syllable *a*, and it has the nature of non-arising because its nature is the *dharmadhātu* and because it is the cause of the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*). "Devoid of vocal utterance" refers to the perspective of Ratnavajrī; "vocal utterance" (*vāgudāhāra*) means the expression of words, and being "devoid" (*varjita*) of that means being free from it, due to the absence of verbal activity through the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*). "The foremost cause of all designations" refers to the gateway of Dharmavajrī.

[269] *Abhilāpa* means verbal expression. The verbal expression of all phenomena, such as the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth, is "all verbal expressions" (*sarvābhilāpa*). The cause or reason for that is the wisdom of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*). For this very reason, it is "supreme" (*agrya*), meaning preeminent. "The brilliant radiance of all speech" refers to its essential nature as the Vajrī of Action. "All speech" (*sarvavāk*) means both "all" and "speech," such as the languages of the gods, the languages of the *nāgas*, and so forth.

For this very reason, it is called "supremely luminous" (*suprabhāsvara*): because manifestations arise within the mental continuums of all sentient beings according to their respective capacities, and because it has the nature of the gnosis that accomplishes activities through the teaching of the Dharma by means of manifold approaches.

Therefore, these four perfections, beginning with Sattvavajrī, are fully established by the four syllables *a*, *ā*, *aṃ*, and *aḥ*. Consequently, that very mind which is by nature the essence of the *dharmadhātu*—being devoid of forms such as subject and object—is of the nature of the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*), because it is luminous due to the absence of adventitious stains and because it serves as the cause for the arising of other types of wisdom. Furthermore, because its nature consists of compassion directed toward phenomena and so forth, and because it does not apprehend distinctions between different mental continua, it is the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*).

The wisdom of discernment arises from being non-erroneous regarding all that is to be known; it consists of the wisdom of accomplishing activities because it is the cause of the welfare of the entire world.
And therefore, in due order, its nature consists of permanence and sovereignty; for this very reason it is said:
"The Greatly Great One, the Great Passion, who brings delight to all sentient beings. (30ab)

"Mahāmahamahārāga," and so forth. Here, the mention of Amitābha at the beginning is for the purpose of demonstrating the primacy of passion (*rāga*). For this very reason, he says: "Passion, hatred, and delusion. At the time of manifesting the worship that pervades all space and all Tathāgatas, it is called "the Great Festival" (*mahāmaha*). By the word *maha*, worship is denoted. *Mahaṇ* means festival; thus, *mahāmaha*. Passion which is of a great nature is "Great Passion" (*mahārāga*). That which is both the Great Festival and Great Passion is "Mahāmahamahārāga."

In this context, "Great Passion" (*mahārāga*) refers to the maturing and liberating of sentient beings; he is the Blessed One, the glorious Vajrasattva, for it is said: "The Blessed One Vajrasattva is indeed the Tathāgata of Great Passion. "He who brings joy to all sentient beings" (*sarvasattvaratikara*) means that he produces joy and delight—in the nature of great bliss—for all sentient beings whose conduct is characterized by passion; thus, he is the one who brings joy to all sentient beings. This is the essential nature of Amitābha. With reference to those whose conduct is characterized by hatred, it is said: [271] "The Great Festival, the Great Hatred, the great enemy of all afflictions. (30cd)

"Mahāmahamahādveṣa" (Great-Great-Mahā-Aversion). "Mahāmaha" has already been explained. Mahādveṣa is Akṣobhya, and he is the great enemy of all afflictions (*kleśa*). The meaning is that he is the great adversary of the primary and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) and so forth. With reference to those whose behavior is dominated by delusion (*moha*), it says: "Mahāmahamahāmoha, the destroyer of the delusion of the deluded mind. (31ab) "Mahāmaha" is as before. Mahāmoha is Vairocana. Delusion of the intellect is *dhīmoha*. That which is both deluded and an intellect-delusion is *mūḍhadhīmoha*; its destroyer (*sūdana*) is the one who annihilates it. With reference to those whose behavior is dominated by anger (*krodha*), it says:
The great festival, the great wrathful one, the great enemy of wrath, the Great One.

"Mahāmahamahākrodha" (Great-Great-Mahākrodha). Likewise, "mahāmaha" is as before. "Mahākrodha" refers to Amoghasiddhi. "Mahākrodharipu mahān" (The Great Enemy of Mahākrodha): because he takes both sentient and non-sentient beings as his object, he is Mahākrodha; he himself is the great enemy of that very [Mahākrodha]. With reference to those whose conduct is dominated by greed (*lobhacarita*), it says: *Mahāmahamahālobhaḥ sarvalobhanisūdanaḥ* (32ab) "Mahāmahamahālobha": "mahāmaha" is as before. "Mahālobha" refers to Ratnasaṃbhava. "Sarvalobhanisūdana" (Destroyer of All Greed): because he serves to purify all mundane and supramundane prosperity.

Because the four gates of liberation, beginning with emptiness, have the sphere of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) as their gateway and serve as the cause for all meditative absorptions; and because that very [sphere] has the aspect of internal emptiness by way of being contrary to internal misconceptions; it has the nature of external emptiness due to the departure from the apprehension of the external; it consists of internal-and-external emptiness by virtue of having the non-apprehension of the body that serves as its basis as its nature; and it possesses the characteristic of great emptiness through the absence of attachment to the receptacle world.
Therefore, it consists of the fourfold meditative absorptions (samādhi) such as Vajrasattva, which are the supports for mirror-like wisdom. Thus it is said:
"He is the great desire, the great bliss, the great joy, and the great delight."

In that context, "Great Desire" (mahākāma) refers to Vajrasattva; "desired" (kāmyate) means desire (kāma), in the sense of that which is to be longed for. "Great Bliss" (mahāsaukhya) refers to Vajrarāja; "Great Joy" (mahāmoda) refers to Vajrarāga; and "Great Delight" (mahāratir) refers to Vajrasādhu.

Precisely for this reason, because the mirror-like gnosis (*ādarśajñāna*) is accomplished through the transformation of the latencies (*vāsanā*) of the eye, forms, and so forth, and because it has as its basis the non-apprehension of the internal and so on; and because these [four foundations of mindfulness], by virtue of being the respective antidotes to error, serve as the causes for the arising of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), its attraction, its attachment, and its state of excellence, respectively. [273]

Thus, because even the knowledge of emptiness (*śūnyatājñāna*) is signless (*animitta*), it is the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatāśūnyatā*). Because there is no grasping at the signs of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), it is the emptiness of the ultimate (*paramārthaśūnyatā*). Because there is no apprehension of the signs of the conditioned accumulation of merit (*saṃskṛtapuṇyasaṃbhāra*), it is the emptiness of the conditioned (*saṃskṛtaśūnyatā*). And because there is no grasping at the signs of the equipment for enlightenment (*bodhisaṃbhāra*) even regarding the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it is the emptiness of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛtaśūnyatā*). For this very reason, he said:
He has a great form, a great body, a great complexion, and a great physique;
he has a great name, is most noble, and possesses a vast and expansive mandala. || 33 ||

In this context, "of great form" (*mahārūpa*) and "of great body" (*mahākāya*) refers to Vajraratna. "Form" (*rūpa*) means that which is manifested, in the sense of being perceived; he whose form is great is "of great form. His greatness consists in his nature as the wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*), because he embodies the consecration into the sovereignty over the Dharma of all Tathāgatas within the triple world. For this very reason, he is "of great body," because he illuminates immeasurable Buddha-fields. "Of great color" (*mahāvarṇa*) and "of great physical presence" (*mahāvapuḥ*) refers to Vajrasūrya. He is "of great color" because he is endowed with the six colors.

He whose body is great is Mahāvapuḥ, because he possesses a circle of radiance consisting of the knowledge arising from the hearing, reflection, and cultivation of the perfectly pure Dharma. He is Mahānāman, meaning "Great Name," and thus Vajraketu; the sense is that he is Mahānāman because his fame is great. Why? Because he has reached the excellence of the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*). And thus he is Mahodāra, "Greatly Noble," being both great and noble because he bestows his very self. He is Mahāvipulamaṇḍala, meaning Vajrahāsa ("Diamond-Laughter").

*Maḍi* means adornment; that which adorns is *maṇḍa*. That which takes (*lāti*) or grasps (*gṛhṇāti*) the *maṇḍa* is a *maṇḍala*. It is vast (*vipula*) and extensive because it pervades all world-systems. That whose essence is a great, vast *maṇḍala* is "one who possesses a great, vast *maṇḍala*," because he brings light to the three worlds.

And therefore, the sequence of those [objects], beginning with the vajra and the jewel, consists of the fourfold set—the knowledge of equality (*samatājñāna*) and its retinue—because, within the knowledge of equality that arises from the transformation of the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭamanas*), the aforementioned signs do not exist by way of the subject (*grāhaka*) and so forth; because they serve as the means for abandoning their respective opposites (*vipakṣa*); and because they are the causes for the attainment of consecration (*abhiṣeka*), the increase of splendor (*tejas*), the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*), the application [to the path], and the accomplishment of joy. Thus is the order of the vajra, the jewel, and the others.

That very [emptiness] is the emptiness of the ultimate (atyanta-śūnyatā) because of the non-adherence to the vow for the welfare of sentient beings as being ultimately real. It is the emptiness of the beginningless and endless (anavarāgra-śūnyatā) because of the non-grasping of the vow, "I must not abandon cyclic existence, which is without beginning or end. It is the emptiness of non-dispersion (anavakāra-śūnyatā) because of the non-adherence to the thought, "I must not fail to apply myself to virtue within the realm of nirvana without remainder. It is the emptiness of nature (prakṛti-śūnyatā) because of the absence of longing, such as "I must purify the lineage (*gotra*) characterized by its intrinsic nature. For this very reason, it has been said:
He who wields the great weapon of wisdom, the supreme goad against the great afflictions;
he of great renown, great fame, great radiance, and great splendor. Thus [it is said]. [34]

In this context, "the bearer of the great weapon of wisdom" refers to Vajradharma. Here, wisdom (*prajñā*) is the gnosis of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*). That itself is the weapon or instrument; he who bears that is the "bearer of the weapon of wisdom. Because his intrinsic nature is that gnosis, he is both "great" and the "bearer of the weapon of wisdom," hence "the bearer of the great weapon of wisdom. "The supreme goad for the great afflictions" refers to Vajratīkṣṇa. The afflictions (*kleśa*) are passion (*rāga*) and so forth. Because he serves as a goad for them, he is the "goad for the afflictions."

He is like a hook (*aṅkuśa*) because he has attained mastery over the afflictions (*kleśa*). Therefore, he is both "great" and a "hook for the afflictions," hence *mahākleśāṅkuśa*. For this very reason, the meaning is that he is the "leader" (*agraṇī*) or the most excellent. He is "of great renown" (*mahāyaśas*) and "of great fame" (*mahākīrti*); this refers to the Vajra-cause, because all the maṇḍala-deities taught in the tantra—who serve as the means for maturing sentient beings—possess the nature of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*). One who possesses great renown is *mahāyaśas*.

For this very reason, he whose fame pervades all world-systems without exception is "Mahākīrti" (of Great Fame). "Mahājyotiḥ" (of Great Light) and "Mahādyutiḥ" (of Great Splendor) refer to the Vajra-speech. He is "Mahājyotiḥ" because his light—his radiance—pervades the three realms extensively. Furthermore, by avoiding the defects of speech—namely, rapidity, slowness, and hesitation—and through the nature of silence during the time of recitation, he is "Mahādyutiḥ" because he illuminates the mental continuums of all sentient beings.

And therefore, because it is based on the discerning wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*) characterized by the transformation of the conceptualizing mind, which has as its intrinsic nature Vajradharma and the others; because, through the discerning wisdom, one discerns the reality of all phenomena by means of the removal of the aforementioned misconceptions; and because, by way of that, it is the cause for the thorough knowledge of the intended meaning of all the irreversible [teachings] regarding the wisdom of the naturally pure reality (*dharmatā-prajñājñāna*); for these very reasons, this is the sequence of these [deities], Vajradharma and the rest. [277]

That very [emptiness] is the emptiness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*) because there is no volitional construction (*anabhisaṃskāra*) regarding the form-body (*rūpakāya*), which consists of the primary and secondary marks. It is the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*) because there is no volitional construction regarding the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), whose intrinsic nature consists of the powers, the grounds of self-confidence, and so forth. It is the emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva-śūnyatā*) because there is no superimposition (*asamāropaṇa*) of a person (*pudgala*) or of phenomena (*dharma*). And it is the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence (*abhāvasvabhāva-śūnyatā*) because there is no volitional construction that denies the characteristics of emptiness as they have been explained. Therefore, he says:

"The wise one who holds the Great Māyā, the accomplisher of the purpose of Great Māyā, he who delights in the passion of Great Māyā, the magician of Great Māyā. [35] In this context, "the wise one who holds the Great Māyā" refers to Vajraviśva. "Māyā" is the emanation of the various, vast, and noble offerings of all the Tathāgatas; he who maintains that is "Māyādhara. He is both great and a holder of Māyā, thus he is "Mahāmāyādhara. For this very reason, he is "wise" (*vidvān*), meaning a scholar (*paṇḍita*), because through those acts of worship he accumulates the equipment of merit (*puṇyasaṃbhāra*). "Accomplisher of the purpose of Great Māyā" refers to Vajrarakṣa. "The purpose of Māyā" means the purpose of emanation (*nirmāṇa*).

He accomplishes and encourages indolent beings; thus, he is the "Accomplisher of Illusory Aims" (*māyārthasādhaka*). He is both great and an accomplisher of illusory aims; thus, he is the "Great Accomplisher of Illusory Aims" (*mahāmāyārthasādhaka*).
