The "Vajrayakṣa" is one who delights in the delight of the Great Illusion (*mahāmāyāratirata*). Delight in illusion is "illusory delight" (*māyārati*); the meaning is that he delights in the emanation of offerings to the Tathāgatas. One who is attached to and devoted to illusory delight is "delighting in illusory delight" (*māyāratirata*). He is both great and one who delights in illusory delight; thus, he is the "Great Delighter in Illusory Delight" (*mahāmāyāratirata*).

"Mahāmāyendrajālika" refers to Vajramuṣṭi. "Māyendrajāla" is the collection of emanations, the unification of the vajras of body, speech, and mind. One who knows that is a "māyendrajālika. He is both great and a *māyendrajālika*, thus he is "Mahāmāyendrajālika. In this context, the absence of the augment [in the compound] is to be understood according to the reading of the *Saddharma* [scripture].
*Sādhayati* likely means ‘to win over’; ‘to guide’ for the *tribe* (kula) is unlikely.

And thus, when the knowledge of the performance of activities (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*)—which consists of the fourfold set beginning with Vajrakarma and is based on the transformation of the consciousnesses of the eye and so forth—exists within oneself, [this occurs] by way of the removal of the aforementioned misconceptions. This is because it serves as the cause for the knowledge of the emptiness of the body and so forth, which brings about the protection of all offerings to the Sugatas and the pacification of obstacles. For this very reason, there is this sequence of these [deities], such as Vajraviśva and the others.

Thus, by virtue of being the antidote to stinginess, immorality, impatience, and laziness, that very [perfection] consists of the perfections of generosity, morality, patience, and vigor. Therefore, it is said:
[279] "The supreme great lord of generosity, the foremost upholder of great morality;
the steadfast upholder of great patience, possessing the prowess of great vigor. [36]

In that regard, "the excellent great lord of givers" refers to Vajralāsyā. That which is given with the desire to perform worship and bestow grace is *dāna* (giving). The lord of that giving is a *dānapati* (lord of givers). Being both great and a lord of givers, he is a *mahādānapati*. He is "excellent" because of his relinquishing of the fourfold giving—consisting of material things (*āmiṣa*), fearlessness (*abhaya*), the Dharma (*dharma*), and empowerment (*abhiṣeka*)—and because he is preeminent over all the world. "The foremost upholder of great ethical discipline" refers to Vajramālā. Ethical discipline (*śīla*) arises from the composure (*samādhāna*) of body, speech, and mind; for the root meaning of the term is "to compose" (*śīla* = *samādhau*).

It has the characteristic of abstaining from the ten unwholesome actions and has the nature of the *prātimokṣa*. One who maintains that is a "holder of ethical discipline" (*śīladhara*). He is both great and a holder of ethical discipline; thus, he is a "great holder of ethical discipline. For this very reason, he is the leader, meaning the one who goes before. "He is a steadfast great holder of patience" (*mahākṣāntidharo dhīraḥ*)—this is from the *Vajragītā*. Patience (*kṣānti*) is the act of enduring or forbearance; one who maintains that is a "holder of patience" (*kṣāntidhara*). He is both great and a holder of patience; thus, he is a "great holder of patience. And for that reason, he is steadfast (*dhīraḥ*).

Because one relies upon fortitude even amidst great sufferings. "Possessing great vigor and prowess" refers to the Vajra Dance. Vigor (*vīrya*) is enthusiasm for what is wholesome; however, enthusiasm for evil and so forth is merely indolence (*kausīdya*) due to its lazy nature, and is not vigor. Its "prowess" (*parākrama*) consists in the fulfillment of all mundane and supramundane roots of virtue.

Furthermore, because it consists of the fourfold secret worship, it sequentially produces the excellence of effortless delight through the power of the purification of one's own doors of liberation during the realization of the mirror-like wisdom and the others.
He says that very same thing by way of its being free from the overcoming of the opposites of faulty wisdom, distraction, and incorrect application.

Abiding in the samādhi of great meditative concentration, bearing the body of great wisdom, possessing great power and great skillful means, he is the vow and the ocean of knowledge. Thus it is said. [37]

In this verse, an exchange between meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) is to be observed. Consequently, the meaning is as follows: "One who bears the body of great wisdom" refers to Vajradhūpā; "great wisdom" (*mahāprajñā*) is wisdom itself, and she is called "one who bears the body of great wisdom" because she sustains that very body. "Abiding in the samādhi of great meditative absorption" refers to Vajrapuṣpā; "samādhi" is characterized by one-pointedness of mind, and "abiding in it" means remaining within that state.

And that meditation is great; thus it is "great meditation" (*mahādhyāna*). Its greatness consists in its being composed of the four meditations (*caturdhyāna*). One who is established in meditative absorption (*samādhistha*) within those four meditations is [the subject]. Regarding "aspiration" (*praṇidhi*): according to Vajradīpā, it is called "aspiration" because one aspires (*praṇidhīyate*). This is because Bodhisattvas arise through the power of their aspirations (*praṇidhāna*). Regarding "great skillful means" (*mahopāya*): according to Vajragandhā, it is "great skillful means" because it is both great and a skillful means.
Precisely by the power of that skillful means, the intentions and inclinations of the entire realm of sentient beings, without exception, are fulfilled according to their wishes.
Therefore, by virtue of being characterized by the perfections of wisdom, meditative concentration, aspiration, and skillful means, it consists of the fourfold external worship.

Because they serve as the cause for the joy of the *sāmbhogika* path and because their intrinsic nature is the entry into the *dharmadhātu*, there is a specific distinction between these two: power (*bala*) and knowledge (*jñāna*). Among them, power consists of the five beginning with faith. Knowledge exists on both the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). Therein, on the path of seeing, it resides in the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*); on the path of cultivation, it resides in the noble eightfold path (*āryāṣṭāṅga*).

And because they consist of faith, vigor, mindfulness, and meditative concentration, they constitute the four gatekeepers, for they are the causes of the great vehicle’s conviction, its engagement, its continuity, and its non-attachment.

Precisely that, with respect to the mere purity of wisdom (*prajñā-pariśuddhi-mātra*), consists of the sixteen meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) beginning with Maitreya, by way of the aforementioned divisions of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Therefore, he says:

[282] "Consisting of great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrīmaya*), immeasurable, possessing great compassion, of supreme intellect; possessing great wisdom, of great intelligence, possessing great skillful means, and of great accomplishment. [38]

In this context, he is Maitreya because he consists of immeasurable great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*). That which possesses a friend (*mitra*) is "friendly" (*maitra*); subsequently, it takes the suffix *ṅi*. Thus, he consists of loving-kindness—that is, his very nature is loving-kindness—toward all sentient beings. He is both "great" and "consisting of loving-kindness," hence "consisting of great loving-kindness. For this very reason, he is immeasurable, because he possesses the love for all beings in the realm of sentient beings as if they were an only son. He is Mañjuśrī because he is "possessed of great compassion and supreme wisdom. Great compassion has the non-referential (*anālambana*) as its essence; he who possesses that is "possessed of great compassion" (*mahākāruṇika*).

"Supreme intellect" (*agradhī*) refers to the knowledge of the perfectly pure realm of phenomena (*suviśuddhadharmadhātujñāna*). From this, it follows that the Blessed One is characterized by both magnificence and profundity. "Of great wisdom" (*mahāprājña*) and "of great intellect" (*mahādhīmān*): Gandhahastin explains that "wisdom" (*prajñā*) consists of the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*); he who possesses such [wisdom] is "wise" (*prājña*). He is "of great wisdom" (*mahāprājña*) because he is both great and wise; for this very reason, he is "of great intellect. "Of great skillful means" (*mahopāya*) and "of great accomplishment" (*mahākṛti*): Jñānaketu explains.

He who possesses a great means is "one of great means" (*mahopāya*). Furthermore, he is "of great accomplishment" (*mahākṛtī*), that is, a great scholar (*mahāpaṇḍita*), because he reveals the true Dharma through his knowledge of the inclinations and latent tendencies of all sentient beings.
Endowed with the power of great supernormal faculties, possessing great speed and great swiftness;
possessed of great supernatural power, of great renown, and of great strength and prowess. Thus. [39]

In this context, "endowed with the power of great supernatural faculties" refers to Bhadrapāla. The power of supernatural faculties is *ṛddhibala*; one who is endowed with that is "endowed with the power of supernatural faculties. One who is both great and endowed with the power of supernatural faculties is "endowed with the power of great supernatural faculties. "Sāgaramati is one of great impulse and great speed. He whose impulse—that is, his movement—is great is "one of great impulse. This is because he travels through many world-systems for the sake of honoring and serving all the Tathāgatas. For this very reason, he is called "one of great speed."

"Of great supernatural power (maharddhika) and of great renown (maheśākhya)" refers to Akṣayamati. He is "of great supernatural power" because he is endowed with the equipment of merit and wisdom (puṇyajñānasaṃbhāra) common to worldly beings, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas. He is "of great renown" because he has brought to full completion the equipment of merit and wisdom of all the Tathāgatas. "Of great strength and prowess (mahābalaparākrama)" refers to Pratibhānakūṭa.

These are "great strengths" (mahānti balāni), namely the ten powers of a Tathāgata, such as the knowledge of what is possible and impossible (sthānāsthānajñāna) and so forth, which will be explained below; he who possesses prowess—that is, the exertion of vigor (vīryārambha)—in these is "of great strength and prowess."
The shatterer of the great mountain of existence, the dense wielder of the great vajra;
the greatly fierce, the greatly terrible, the one who causes fear even to the fearful. Thus. [40]

In this context, "the shatterer of the great mountain of existence" (*mahābhavādrisaṃbhetta*) refers to Mahāsthāmaprāpta. "Existence" (*bhava*) consists of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandhāḥ*). These themselves are a "mountain" because they are a mountain of ignorance. One who has the nature of shattering it—by virtue of attaining correct, non-erroneous knowledge—is a "shatterer. Being both "great" and a "shatterer of the mountain of existence," he is the "Great Shatterer of the Mountain of Existence. "The dense Great Vajra-holder" (*mahāvajradharo ghanaḥ*) refers to Sarvāpāyañjaha. He is a "Great Vajra-holder" because he holds the Great Vajra, which is the wisdom of Samantabhadra.

He is "Dense" (*ghana*) because of his compactness and his possession of form. He is "Greatly Fierce" (*mahākrūra*) and "Greatly Terrible" (*mahāraudra*); this refers to the mind that destroys all sorrow and darkness. He is "Greatly Fierce" because he is both great and fierce, manifesting a form of great wrath for the sake of beings who are difficult to subdue. He is "Greatly Terrible" because although the Blessed Lord Mañjuśrī is peaceful, he displays ferocity by virtue of disciplining sentient beings. He is "The Terrifier of Great Fear" (*mahābhayabhayaṃkara*), which is Jālinīprabha.
"Mahābhaya" means one who possesses a most terrifying form; "Śaṃkara" is he who causes fear even to him, thus he is "Mahābhayabhayaṅkara."
"The Lord who is the supreme great vidyā, the Guru who is the supreme great mantra;
he who has ascended the way of the Mahāyāna, the supreme of the Mahāyāna way.

[41] In this context, "the Lord who is the supreme great vidyā" refers to Candraprabha. These are the "great vidyās"—that is, the four dhāraṇīs consisting of text, meaning, mantra, and mudrā. He is the supreme among them; for this very reason, he is the "Lord," because he completely purifies the bodily, vocal, and mental conduct of all sentient beings from all states of woe. "The Guru who is the supreme great mantra" refers to Amitaprabha.

"Mahāmantra" means that which is both great and a mantra; it is the supreme and most excellent, meaning it consists of the Great Seal (mahāmudrā). For this very reason, he is the "Guru" of all sentient beings because he teaches the realization (abhisamaya) through his knowledge of their inclinations and latent tendencies. He is "mounted on the system of the Mahāyāna," meaning Gaganagañja; the meaning is that he is mounted upon—that is, established in—the "system" or path of the Mahāyāna, which will be explained below. [286]

"The supreme method of the Mahāyāna" refers to Sarvanivaraṇaviṣkambhin. Because one realizes the ineffable nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) regarding both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpaka-jñāna*) is the Mahāyāna. Alternatively, the Mahāyāna is summarized by its threefold unsurpassedness as having the accumulations, the means, the sphere of activity, the support, and the intrinsic nature. If this is so, how is it "great"? The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are for the benefit of the entire world; therefore, they are "great. This vehicle belongs to them, either for their perfection or for their departure [to liberation].

Therefore, the Mahāyāna is the vehicle for those who possess these [qualities]. Alternatively, it is the Mahāyāna because it is the vehicle of the great ones (*mahatām*). Or else, it is the Mahāyāna because of its sevenfold greatness: the greatness of objective support (*ālambana*), practice (*pratipatti*), knowledge (*jñāna*), vigor (*vīrya*), skill in means (*upāyakauśalya*), attainment (*samudāgama*), and activity (*karman*). It is called the Mahāyāna because it is both "great" (*mahat*) and a "vehicle" (*yāna*); for such qualities do not exist in other vehicles. This threefold Mahāyāna, in relation to cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), should be understood as being for the purpose of fully illuminating the cause, the sphere of activity, and the intrinsic nature.

Thus, because he depends solely upon skillful means and because he possesses the nature of all mundane and supramundane meditative absorptions, the Blessed One, the Gnosis-being, is the Gnosis-body of the Tathāgata.

Thus, by means of these names, mantra-syllables, and phrases—beginning with "The Blessed One, the Buddha, the Fully Awakened One, born from the syllable A"—which are distinguished by their qualifiers, devoid of finite verbs, and serve as terms of apprehension, the qualified Jñānasattva Mañjuśrī, who dwells in the hearts of all Tathāgatas and is the foremost among the glorious ones, is to be perceived.

And those deities of the maṇḍala, such as Vajrasattva and the others, emerge through the yoga of Mahāmudrā, endowed with their respective colors and syllables; having emerged, they perform the Buddha-activities for sentient beings throughout all world-systems, and returning once more, they become the syllables of the name-mantras, colored by the specific color of their own family.

Having visualized, in due order, the deities as established within the moon-maṇḍalas previously arranged in the great maṇḍala of the Vajradhātu, and having resolved that one's own self is Mañjuśrī-jñānasattva—the embodiment of the gnosis of all Tathāgatas—residing at the hub of that wheel, with a form as previously described; then, whoever, whether a son of noble family or a daughter of noble family, practices the conduct of the mantra-vehicle, should recite the *Nāmasaṃgīti*, the crest-jewel of the non-dual ultimate reality of that very Blessed One, the embodiment of gnosis.
The Bodhisattvas will recite it three times from memory, or, reading it from a book, they will set it in motion.

Having become pure and observant of silence, by reciting the syllables and words of the name-mantra correctly while remaining in a state of quietude such that no one hears them, one will before long attain the multitude of qualities enumerated among the benefits as well as others.

This bull among men, who upholds the *Paramārthanāmasaṃgīti*, having well-accumulated the equipment of merit and wisdom, will very swiftly perfect all the qualities of a Buddha and realize unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. For many eons, he shall not pass into parinirvāṇa; he is the teacher of the unsurpassed Dharma for all sentient beings, the drum of the Dharma in the ten directions, and the King of Dharma.

Regarding this Great Maṇḍala of the Vajra Realm, there are eighty-six names formed by combining the syllables and words of its name-mantras into one. These are to be applied by distributing them among the deities of the maṇḍala. Among them, four pertain to the Wisdom Being (jñānasattva) and the moon-maṇḍala; three to the letter *a*; five to Sattvavajrī and the others; and eleven to Śaśvata and the others.

Starting from Vajrasattva up to Sarvanivaraṇaviṣkambhin, all the remaining name-mantra syllables and words should be joined in their proper sequence according to the relationship of qualifier and qualified. There are fourteen verses; the name-mantra syllables are eighty-six even by count—this is the traditional teaching.
In the *Āryanāmasaṃgītiṭīkā*, titled *Nāmamantrārthāvalokinī*, the fifth chapter, concerning the Great Maṇḍala of the Vajradhātu by Bodhicittavajra, is concluded.
